cards.explanation: The answer is the Israelites. God speaks to Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), and Aaron, the priest (Exodus 28:1): “Say to the Israelites…” (Leviticus 15:2). So the Israelites are the people this message is addressed to. That's a big audience, and God names it plainly. I think that's a pretty clear way to run things.

The answer is that it's unclean. God says, “…the discharge is unclean.” (Leviticus 15:2). He doesn't call it a curse or a punishment. He names it unclean and then spells out what to do about it. I like a clear recipe, friends.

The answer is to wash his clothes and bathe with water. Right there in verse 5: “Anyone who touches his bed must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.” So it's a wash, a bath, and then a wait until evening. That's the whole list, bakers. It's not a big production, just a clear one.

The answer is False. Verse 9 says, “Any saddle on which the man with the discharge rides will be unclean.” Beds, furniture, and now saddles. This list is getting longer than a to-do list on a Monday morning.

The answer is when he didn't rinse his hands first, and the key word is “without.” Verse 11 says, “If the man with the discharge touches anyone without first rinsing his hands with water, the one who was touched must wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he will be unclean until evening.” So the rinse is what matters, friends. Rinsed hands first, and the verse doesn't send that person to the washtub.
The answer is broken. Verse 12 says, “Any clay pot that the man with the discharge touches must be broken…” Ouch. Clay pots had a rough day in that camp. Nobody threw a party for the pot.
The answer is False. Verse 12 says the clay pot must be broken, but the wooden utensil “…must be rinsed with water.” Two materials, two instructions. The wooden utensil gets off easy, friends.

The answer is fresh water. Verse 13 says he must “…bathe himself in fresh water, and he shall be clean.” The passage names the water. Seven days counted, clothes washed, fresh water. And then on the eighth day come the two turtledoves or two young pigeons (verse 14).

The answer is the priest. Verse 14 says he is to take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, come before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, “…and give them to the priest.” The priest is the one who carries it from there. The man's job is to show up with the birds, friends.

The answer is a sin offering and a burnt offering. Verse 15 says, “The priest is to sacrifice them, one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering.” One bird for each. Then the verse says the priest “…will make atonement for the man before the LORD because of his discharge.”

The answer is False. For an emission of semen, verse 16 says the man “…must bathe his whole body with water, and he will be unclean until evening.” No eighth day, no birds. The birds belong to the discharge case before it, friends.

The answer is False. Verse 18 says, “…both must bathe with water, and they will remain unclean until evening.” So the woman bathes too, and both are unclean until evening. The law counts them together.

The answer is seven. Verse 19 says, “…she will be unclean due to her menstruation for seven days, and anyone who touches her will be unclean until evening.” Seven is the number for this one, bakers. The passage doesn't hand out numbers carelessly.

The answer is that they're unclean until evening. Verse 19 says, “…anyone who touches her will be unclean until evening.” That's for the person who touches her, and it ends at evening. It's the same waiting time you've seen all through this passage, friends.

The answer is False. Verse 24 says, “…he will be unclean for seven days, and any bed on which he lies will become unclean.” So it's seven days, not just until evening. The bed he lies on is unclean too.

The answer is all the days of her discharge. Verse 25 says, “…she will be unclean all the days of her unclean discharge, just as she is during the days of her menstruation.” So there's no set number of days for this one, friends. After she is cleansed, she counts off seven days, and then she will be ceremonially clean (verse 28).

The answer is so they don't die by making His tabernacle unclean, and this is where God finally says it outright. Verse 31: “You must keep the children of Israel separate from their uncleanness, so that they do not die by defiling My tabernacle, which is among them.” So it's about His tabernacle, and it's serious. This is the reason behind all that washing, bakers.
The answer is False. God says, “…My tabernacle, which is among them.” (Leviticus 15:31). So His tabernacle is among His people, not far off. I think that's the best part of the whole verse, friends.

The answer is True. Verse 33 lists “…any male or female who has a discharge…” So the law covers both men and women. The list is long, and nobody is left out, friends. That's the end of this whole group on clean and unclean.
